strengths: The paper addresses an important practical computer-vision problem: preserving diffusion-model generation quality under very low activation precision. Treating the submission as Algorithms/General, the proposed activation-side Hadamard preconditioning is intuitive and relevant.

The empirical gains over EfficientDM are substantial in difficult settings. On ImageNet LDM-4, W4A3 improves IS from 8.74 to 49.62 and FID from 99.78 to 33.47; improvements are also reported on LSUN-Bedrooms and LSUN-Churches.

Evaluation covers conditional and unconditional generation, three dataset/model combinations, several weight/activation precisions, 50,000 generated samples, and multiple complementary metrics including FID, sFID, precision, recall, and IS.

The paper provides useful activation-distribution visualizations across layers and timesteps, and the qualitative samples support the claim that HQ-DM degrades less severely than EfficientDM at low activation precision.
weaknesses: The central hardware-efficiency claim is not adequately demonstrated. There are no latency, throughput, memory, energy, kernel, or deployment measurements on actual hardware, nor an accounting of the two online Hadamard operations surrounding activation quantization. Accumulator widths and the bit width of the transformed integer tensor supplied to convolution are also unspecified.

The method lacks decisive component ablations. The paper varies only Hadamard order and does not compare no transformation, single versus double transformation, fixed versus timestep-learned scales, symmetric baselines, or variants with and without LoRA. Consequently, the reported gains cannot be attributed specifically to the claimed innovation.

Several technical statements are inaccurate or insufficiently justified. Equation 19 is false as written for an arbitrary standard basis vector: a Hadamard row has constant magnitude but is not generally the all-ones vector. The raw Hadamard matrix is dense, not sparse as claimed. The treatment of channel dimensions not divisible by the chosen block size and the rationale for applying the convolutional transform along spatial width are also incomplete.

Reproducibility is weak. Although the text says more details are in an appendix, no experimental appendix is provided. Important information is missing, including training iterations and compute, learning rates, LoRA rank and placement, scale granularity and initialization, calibration or synthetic-data construction, exact quantized layer coverage, random seeds, and evaluation-statistics implementation.

Baseline fairness is unclear. HQ-DM uses symmetric activation quantization whereas EfficientDM is described as asymmetric, but there is no controlled reimplementation isolating this difference. Baseline provenance, identical training budgets, and whether all metrics were recomputed under one evaluation pipeline are not established.

Some claims overstate the evidence. The reported 467.73% relative IS gain arises from an extremely weak W4A3 baseline and still leaves a large gap to the full-precision IS. The claim of greater than 100% improvement across all four metrics is mathematically inappropriate for lower-is-better metrics and is inconsistent with the stated approximately 99.7% precision improvement. Overall, the promising benchmark results support a close decision, but missing hardware validation, core ablations, and implementation detail slightly favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem—low-bit quantization of diffusion models—and proposes a simple activation-rotation mechanism that can be integrated with LoRA-based QAT. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/bfbb76a614cc48549a1435355b561ad2/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Experiments cover conditional and unconditional generation on ImageNet and two LSUN datasets, use 50,000 generated samples, and report several complementary metrics.

The reported gains over EfficientDM are substantial in difficult low-activation-bit settings. For example, ImageNet W4A3 improves from 8.74 to 49.62 IS and from 99.78 to 33.47 FID; improvements also appear on both LSUN datasets.
The authors provide an ablation over Hadamard order and visualize activation statistics and generated samples.
weaknesses: The central technical presentation contains consequential errors and ambiguities. Equation (19) claims every standard basis vector maps to an all-positive constant vector under a Hadamard matrix; generally, it maps to a row containing both positive and negative signs, although the magnitudes are constant. The text also calls the raw Hadamard matrix sparse even though it is dense. These mistakes undermine confidence in the supporting argument.

The claimed hardware efficiency is not demonstrated. There are no latency, throughput, memory, energy, operation-count, or hardware-kernel measurements. The proposed path applies a Hadamard transform before quantization and an inverse transform afterward, while the convolution construction transforms the spatial width dimension. The paper does not convincingly show that this realizes a faster end-to-end integer convolution or accounts for transform and scale-handling overhead.

The empirical design does not isolate the proposed contribution. There is no ablation comparing the complete system against the same QAT framework without Hadamard rotation, double rotation, randomized/sign-adjusted Hadamard rotation, symmetric-quantization-only controls, or alternative activation-smoothing methods. Varying only the Hadamard order cannot establish which component causes the gains.

The comparison set is incomplete for an ECCV 2026 submission. Recent methods cited by the paper itself, including 2025 diffusion-quantization approaches, are omitted from the tables; EfficientDM from 2024 is effectively the sole complete QAT baseline. It is also unclear whether baselines were rerun under identical training, quantization, and evaluation protocols.

Reproducibility is poor. Despite referring readers to an appendix, the appendix supplies almost no implementation details: LoRA rank, learning rates, training iterations, batch size, scale initialization and parameterization, training/calibration data, layer coverage, compute budget, and random seeds are missing. No code or release commitment is stated.

The paper reports single numbers without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. This is important because several improvements outside the extreme W4A3 case are modest, and FID/IS can vary with sampling and evaluation details.

Some quantitative claims are incorrect or exaggerated. The statement that all four ImageNet W4A3 metrics improve by more than 100% is not supported: the relative reductions in FID and sFID are below 100%, and precision improves by approximately 99.7%. Claims of exceptional performance and strong generalization therefore exceed the evidence.

The novelty is limited: the method largely combines an EfficientDM-style LoRA distillation framework and timestep-dependent scales with a Hadamard sandwich around activation quantization. The paper does not adequately distinguish this from established rotation-based quantization beyond avoiding transformed weights.

Presentation and attribution need substantial revision. The paper incorrectly attributes timestep-aware scales to generic LSQ, contains duplicate references, includes placeholder or incomplete bibliographic entries, and has numerous terminology and writing problems. Overall, the reported empirical signal is promising, but the technical inaccuracies, missing controls, inadequate contemporary comparisons, and unsupported hardware claims make the case for acceptance unconvincing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical computer-vision problem: preserving diffusion-model generation quality under very low-bit weight and activation quantization. The proposed activation rotation is simple, compatible with the existing LoRA-based QAT framework, and targets a clearly motivated failure mode—heavy-tailed, timestep-varying activations.

The empirical improvements are substantial in the most challenging settings. On ImageNet with LDM-4, W4A3 improves IS from 8.74 to 49.62 and FID from 99.78 to 33.47 over EfficientDM. Consistent W4A3 gains are also reported on LSUN-Bedrooms and LSUN-Churches, suggesting that the method is not tailored to a single dataset.

The evaluation covers conditional and unconditional generation, three datasets, two LDM configurations, several bit-width combinations, 50,000 generated samples per setting, and multiple complementary metrics. The activation-distribution plots and qualitative results support the proposed outlier-smoothing mechanism.

Avoiding offline Hadamard transformation of quantized weights is a reasonable design choice. The analysis and Figure 3 provide an intuitive explanation for why rotating relatively uniform weights can create new extremes, while the order ablation gives some evidence about the transformation design.

The manuscript is generally well organized and clearly illustrates the method and its observed low-bit advantages. Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, it offers a useful and potentially deployable extension of diffusion-model QAT.
weaknesses: The central hardware-efficiency claim is not demonstrated experimentally. There are no latency, throughput, memory, energy, operation-count, or accelerator measurements, despite repeated claims of efficient integer matrix multiplication and convolution. The online forward and inverse Hadamard operations introduce overhead whose practical cost is not quantified.

Important implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing: LoRA rank, learning rates, training budget and compute, quantizer granularity, scale initialization, calibrated layers or exclusions, accumulator precision, intermediate requantization, and the precise data-free sampling procedure. The text refers readers to an appendix, but the supplied manuscript provides no corresponding experimental appendix or code information.

The convolution formulation requires further justification. It reshapes activations and applies the transform along the spatial width dimension, then applies an inverse transform before convolution. The paper does not analyze padding, stride, varying resolution, numerical range, overflow, or whether the resulting computation actually accelerates standard convolution kernels. Moreover, the statement that the raw Hadamard matrix is sparse is incorrect—it is dense, although it admits a fast transform.

Some claims overstate the tables. HQ-DM does not outperform all alternatives across all metrics: for ImageNet W8A4, EfficientDM has better FID and sFID; for W4A4, QuEST has better FID. The statement that W4A3 improves all four metrics by more than 100% is also mathematically inappropriate for lower-is-better metrics and is inconsistent with the reported values.

The ablation evidence is narrow. The paper varies only Hadamard order and does not isolate Single Hadamard transformation from timestep-wise learned scales and LoRA training, compare directly against a properly implemented Double Hadamard baseline, report run-to-run variability, or test whether simpler clipping or smoothing baselines yield similar gains.

Novelty is moderate: Hadamard-based activation smoothing and LoRA-based QAT are established ingredients, while the main contribution is their particular combination and placement for diffusion models. Given the missing system validation and incomplete ablations, the evidence supports a borderline rather than confident acceptance.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: accurate low-bit weight-and-activation quantization of diffusion models, where timestep-dependent distributions and activation outliers make aggressive quantization difficult.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad, covering conditional and unconditional generation, three datasets/resolutions, U-Net-based LDMs, Transformer-based DiT-XL, several bit-widths, and multiple generation metrics using 50,000 samples.

Reported gains over EfficientDM are substantial in difficult settings. For example, ImageNet LDM-4 W4A3 improves IS from 8.74 to 49.62 and FID from 99.78 to 33.47; improvements also appear on both LSUN datasets and DiT-XL.

The component ablation separates LSQ, LoRA, and Hadamard transformation, while the comparison against a double-Hadamard variant attempts to isolate the proposed transformation design. The use of symmetric activation quantization is also practically motivated.
weaknesses: The central hardware-efficiency claim is not convincingly established. Equations 12 and 14 still require applying an online inverse Hadamard transform between low-bit activation quantization and the linear/convolution operation. The paper does not explain fusion, accumulator precision, intermediate bit width, memory traffic, or whether the transformed activation remains an A-bit representation at the actual convolution input. Calling the method fully W4A4 and directly hardware-friendly therefore needs substantially more justification.

The manuscript incorrectly describes the raw Hadamard matrix as sparse; it is a dense matrix of plus/minus one entries. Efficient implementation would require a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform, but its implementation, cost, supported tensor shapes, padding, and comparison with optimized integer kernels are not documented.

The convolution construction is weakly motivated: it rotates the spatial width dimension, reconstructs it online, and then performs convolution. The assertion that conventional double-Hadamard transformation is inherently incompatible with convolution is not demonstrated and overlooks standard channel-wise rotations that can be folded into convolution kernels. Moreover, the reported DHQ-DM baseline replaces its convolution layers with the proposed single-transform scheme, so Table 6 is not a clean test of the claimed incompatibility.

Efficiency evidence is inadequate for a systems-facing claim. Only end-to-end latency on one unspecified implementation and A100 setup is reported, with speedup measured against the authors' unusually poor DHQ-DM baseline rather than FP32, EfficientDM, or optimized INT kernels. There are no kernel-level measurements, throughput, memory, energy, hardware utilization, or deployment results.

Reproducibility is poor. Essential settings—including Hadamard block order, treatment of incompatible dimensions, quantization granularity, LoRA rank and placement, learning rates, epochs/iterations, training inputs, scale initialization, batch sizes, and precise latency protocol—are absent. The text repeatedly refers to an appendix, but the supplied manuscript contains no appendix, and no code or implementation details are provided.

Several claims overstate or misinterpret the tables. The statement that W4A3 improves all four metrics by more than 100% is not meaningful for lower-is-better metrics and is numerically false under ordinary relative-reduction definitions. The abstract emphasizes a 467.73% relative IS increase from a severely degraded baseline, which obscures that the resulting IS of 49.62 remains far below the FP score of 365.35.

The evidence for the proposed mechanism is limited. Activation smoothing and weight-outlier amplification are illustrated using a few layers or a single weight tensor, without layer/timestep-wide statistics, sensitivity to block size, quantization-error analysis, or qualitative generated samples. Thus, the large metric gains are not yet tied convincingly to the claimed mechanism.

The method is largely a combination of known Hadamard smoothing, LSQ timestep-aware scales, and EfficientDM-style LoRA distillation. The distinction from prior rotation-based quantization is relatively modest, and the paper lacks sufficiently rigorous hardware or analytical validation to elevate that distinction into a convincing ECCV contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: preserving diffusion-model generation quality under low-bit weight and activation quantization.

The evaluation spans conditional and unconditional generation, U-Net and Transformer backbones, three datasets, several bit-widths, and 50,000 generated samples per evaluation. The reported gains over EfficientDM are often substantial, especially for 3-bit activations.

The component ablation indicates that the Hadamard transformation can improve multiple training variants, while the activation and weight distribution plots provide some intuition for the proposed design.
weaknesses: The central hardware-efficiency claim is not technically established. Equations 12–14 still require an online inverse Hadamard transform before the linear or convolution operation. Its sums generally have greater bit width than the advertised A-bit activations, so it is unclear whether standard W4A4/W4A3 integer kernels can execute the stated computation or whether the bit-width labels reflect the actual convolution inputs.

The mathematical exposition contains consequential errors. Equation 15 is false for an arbitrary standard-basis vector: only the first Hadamard row is all positive, while other rows contain signs. More seriously, the paper repeatedly calls the raw Hadamard matrix “sparse,” although it is a dense ±1 matrix. These errors undermine the explanation of both outlier smoothing and computational cost.

Efficiency evidence is inadequate for an Applied/Systems-style hardware claim. Latency is compared only with the authors' Double-Hadamard variant, not FP32, EfficientDM, or optimized low-bit baselines. The implementation backend, accumulator precision, transform order, kernel fusion, batching, warm-up, and measurement protocol are unspecified; memory, throughput, and energy are not reported. The Double-Hadamard baseline also collapses even at W8A8, raising concerns about whether it is a meaningful implementation.

The method is not reproducible from the manuscript. It omits LoRA rank and placement, learning rates, optimizer schedule, number and construction of distillation samples, training iterations, Hadamard block sizes, transformed layers, scale granularity, clipping initialization, and most latency settings. The text points to an appendix, but the supplied 18-page manuscript contains no appendix or implementation details.

The empirical evidence lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, and qualitative generated samples. The outlier analysis covers only a few layers at one timestep, while the weight analysis uses a single tensor; this is insufficient to support broad claims about timestep-dependent activation outliers or systematic weight degradation.

Several claims misstate the tables. For W4A3, FID and sFID reductions cannot be described as improvements “exceeding 100%,” and the precision increase is about 99.7%, not over 100%. Large inconsistencies among IS, FID, and the full-precision reference—such as quantized models obtaining much better FID but dramatically worse IS—are not investigated.

The novelty is limited: HQ-DM largely combines existing LoRA distillation, timestep-aware LSQ, and Hadamard activation rotation. A single-sided rotation may be useful, but the manuscript does not rigorously distinguish it from simply quantizing in a rotated basis or analyze when it should outperform prior smoothing methods.

Overall, the reported accuracy gains are promising, but incorrect technical statements, ambiguity about the true arithmetic precision, and insufficient systems and reproducibility evidence prevent a convincing case for the paper's principal claims.

strengths: HQ-DM addresses an important deployment bottleneck for diffusion models: severe activation outliers under low-bit quantization. Applying the Hadamard transform only to activations is a simple, practically motivated modification of existing LoRA-based QAT.

The empirical results are consistently favorable across several settings. Gains are reported on ImageNet, LSUN-Bedrooms, and LSUN-Churches; on both U-Net-based LDMs and Transformer-based DiT; and especially under challenging W4A4 and W4A3 quantization.

The component ablation in Table 5 provides useful evidence that the Hadamard transform contributes beyond timestep-aware scales and LoRA distillation. The comparison with the double-transform variant also supports the motivation for avoiding transformed weights.

Evaluation uses 50,000 generated images and multiple complementary metrics, including FID, sFID, Inception Score, precision, and recall. This is substantially stronger than relying on a single generative-quality metric.
The paper is generally easy to follow, motivates activation outliers clearly, and connects the proposed design to integer arithmetic and convolutional architectures.
weaknesses: The implementation and reproducibility details are seriously incomplete. The manuscript does not specify essential hyperparameters such as LoRA rank, learning rates, training iterations, Hadamard block orders, quantization granularity, scale initialization, calibration or distillation data, and layer exclusions. It refers readers to an appendix, but no appendix is included in the supplied manuscript.

The hardware-efficiency case is not adequately established. Table 6 measures speed only relative to a constructed double-Hadamard variant, not against FP32, EfficientDM, or optimized INT baselines. There are no memory, throughput, energy, kernel, or hardware details demonstrating that the proposed integer formulation yields an end-to-end deployment advantage. Calling the dense Hadamard matrix “sparse” is also technically inaccurate unless the authors specifically mean a factored fast Walsh-Hadamard implementation.

Equation (15) is mathematically incorrect as written: for a general standard basis vector, a row of a Sylvester Hadamard matrix contains both positive and negative entries rather than being the all-ones vector. Its magnitudes are uniform, so the intuition may be repairable, but the formal argument needs correction.

Some conclusions are overstated. For W4A3 in Table 1, the paper claims improvements exceeding 100% across all four metrics, although FID and sFID reductions are approximately 66% and 82%, and precision improves by about 100%. Such percentage reporting is also potentially misleading when mixing higher-is-better and lower-is-better metrics.

The comparison with double Hadamard transformation is not fully controlled because convolutional layers in that baseline are reverted to the proposed single-transform scheme. Moreover, the paper offers only a single-layer analysis of transformed-weight outliers and provides no uncertainty estimates or repeated-run results.

For an image-generation paper, the absence of qualitative samples or failure-case analysis makes it difficult to assess perceptual artifacts behind the aggregate scores. Limitations are also not discussed explicitly. Overall, the results support a promising contribution, but incomplete reproducibility and insufficient validation of the central hardware claims keep the recommendation at borderline accept.
